tasks.summary:
The root cause of the failure was that the `LRUCache` implementation did not correctly update the order of keys when `get()` was called, failing to meet the requirement that a `get()` operation should count as a "use" to maintain the Least Recently Used (LRU) order. Furthermore, the `put()` operation did not handle updates to existing keys correctly, as it could unnecessarily evict an item if the key already existed.

I updated the `LRUCache` class to:
1.  In `get()`, pop and re-insert the accessed key to move it to the "most recently used" position (end of the dictionary).
2.  In `put()`, correctly handle existing keys by deleting them first before re-inserting them, ensuring they are also moved to the "most recently used" position and preventing incorrect eviction if the cache is at capacity.

The root cause of the issue was that `InventoryService.reserve` did not persist changes to the repository after updating the item's stock. Since the `InMemoryRepository` returns a copy of the item, modifying the returned object did not affect the data stored in the repository.

Additionally, `InventoryService.reserve_many` was calling `self.reserve` in a loop. Because `reserve` modifies the repository directly, if one of the SKUs in `reserve_many` failed (e.g., due to `OutOfStock`), the previous successful reservations in the same `reserve_many` call had already been committed to the repository, violating the "all-or-nothing" requirement.

I fixed these issues by:
1. Updating `InventoryService.reserve` to save the modified item back to the repository.
2. Refactoring `InventoryService.reserve_many` to perform all necessary checks before applying any changes to the repository, ensuring atomicity.
